title: Using Identities to Elevate Team Member Engagement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explores a persuasion technique: reframing a request for action into an identity a person is asked to embody. Rather than asking someone to innovate, a leader asks them to be an Innovator; rather than asking them to lead, a leader asks them to be a Leader. The essay argues identities feel more permanent than one-off actions and tap into self-image, self-esteem, and self-worth in ways that plain requests don't. It cites author Jonah Berger's line that being labeled a 'cheater' or 'loser' feels worse than an isolated act of cheating or losing, and closes with a small illustrative example of asking a colleague to be a 'friend' rather than simply asking for help.
points: Reframing action-requests as identity-requests ('be an Innovator' vs. 'innovate') taps a deeper psychological lever than task assignment alone.
Identities feel more permanent than actions, which is why people work harder to live up to them once named.
The technique works both by pull (wanting to be seen as the positive identity) and by push (not wanting to be seen as its negative counterpart).
Jonah Berger's framing — that being a 'cheater' feels worse than cheating once — is used to explain why identity language outperforms action language.
The essay offers a concrete vocabulary of action-to-identity swaps (collaboration to Collaborator, strategy to Strategist, teach to Coach) leaders can reuse.
quotes: To increase the odds that team members will embrace their calls for action with more vigor and enthusiasm, great leaders have learned a secret. They turn their requests for action into identities that people must live up to.
Consider the difference between describing someone as learning versus describing that person as a learner. The persona of a learner seems more permanent and more likely to persist.
For example, instead of asking a team member to innovate, they ask them to be an Innovator. Rather than ask them to be more decisive, they ask them to be the Decision-Maker.
As author and proponent of this idea, Jonah Berger likes to say, “Cheating is bad, but being a cheater is worse. Losing is bad, but being a loser is worse.
So, the next time you get in a jam, don’t ask a colleague to help you. Instead, ask them to be a “friend and pitch in.” You’ll likely find they lend a hand with a lot more enthusiasm.
